units.title: Composition and Mass Spectra
units.blurb: The mass laws that pointed to atoms, mass spectra, and formulas from chemical analysis.

units.title: Light and the Quantum Atom
units.blurb: Waves and photons, hydrogen's energy levels, quantum numbers and photoelectron spectra.

units.title: Explaining Periodic Trends
units.blurb: Coulomb's law, shielding and effective nuclear charge explain each trend and its exceptions.

units.title: Bonding and Molecular Structure
units.blurb: Bond energy curves, lattice energy, formal charge, resonance, shapes, hybrid orbitals and molecular orbitals.

units.title: Liquids, Solids and Phase Changes
units.blurb: Compare intermolecular forces, vapor pressure and phase diagrams, look inside crystals, and separate mixtures.

units.title: Solutions and Colligative Properties
units.blurb: Ions in solution, the energy of dissolving, more ways to state concentration, light absorption, and properties that depend only on the number of solute particles.

units.title: Gases in Depth
units.blurb: Gas density, gas stoichiometry, mixtures of gases, molecular speeds and real gases.

units.title: Reactions in Solution
units.blurb: Net ionic equations, solution stoichiometry, titrations, oxidation numbers and redox.

units.title: Thermochemistry
units.blurb: Energy bookkeeping for reactions: the first law, enthalpy, calorimetry, Hess's law and enthalpies of formation.

topics.title: Definite and Multiple Proportions
topics.short: A compound has a fixed mass ratio of elements; when two elements make several compounds, their mass ratios compare as small whole numbers.
topics.trouble: Students compare the total masses of oxygen in two compounds instead of the oxygen that combines with a fixed mass of the other element.

topics.title: Mass Spectra of Elements
topics.short: Each peak is an isotope: its position gives the mass and its height gives the abundance.
topics.trouble: Students read the mass of the tallest peak as the average atomic mass, or add the peak masses without weighting them.

topics.title: Combustion Analysis
topics.short: Burn a compound, weigh the CO₂ and H₂O, and work back to its empirical formula.
topics.trouble: Students forget that the compound's oxygen must be found by subtracting, since the products also hold oxygen that came from the O₂.

topics.title: Composition of Mixtures
topics.short: Use the measured mass of one element to find how much of each compound a mixture holds.
topics.trouble: Students treat a mixture as if it had one fixed formula, or apply one compound's percent composition to the whole mixture.

topics.title: Wavelength, Frequency and the Spectrum
topics.short: Light's speed is its wavelength times its frequency: c = λν.
topics.trouble: Students think a longer wavelength means a higher frequency, or forget to change nanometers to meters.

topics.title: Photons and the Photoelectric Effect
topics.short: Light comes in packets of energy E = hν, and only photons above a threshold frequency can free an electron from a metal.
topics.trouble: Students think brighter light gives each photon more energy, so a bright red beam should free electrons that a dim violet one can.

topics.title: Hydrogen's Energy Levels
topics.short: Eₙ = −2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J / n², and each spectral line is a jump between two levels.
topics.trouble: Students think the levels get farther apart as n grows, when they crowd together, or report a negative wavelength for an emission line.

topics.title: What Light Does to Molecules
topics.short: Microwaves set molecules rotating, infrared makes bonds vibrate, and visible and ultraviolet light move electrons to higher levels.
topics.trouble: Students think infrared light makes electrons jump between levels, or that any light can break any bond.

topics.title: Quantum Numbers
topics.short: The numbers n, l, mₗ and mₛ name an electron's shell, subshell, orbital and spin.
topics.trouble: Students allow l to equal n, or think mₗ can only be positive.

topics.title: Orbital Diagrams and Magnetism
topics.short: Pauli's rule and Hund's rule place the arrows, and unpaired electrons make an atom paramagnetic.
topics.trouble: Students pair electrons in one p orbital before every orbital in the sublevel has one, and so miscount the unpaired electrons.

topics.title: Configurations of Ions and Exceptions
topics.short: Transition metals lose their 4s electrons first, and chromium and copper break the filling pattern.
topics.trouble: Students remove 3d electrons before 4s ones when they form Fe²⁺.

topics.title: Photoelectron Spectroscopy
topics.short: Each peak shows the energy needed to remove electrons from one subshell, and its height counts those electrons.
topics.trouble: Students read a taller peak as a higher energy rather than more electrons, or forget that the highest binding energies belong to the electrons nearest the nucleus.

topics.title: Coulomb's Law in Atoms
topics.short: The attraction between charges grows with the size of the charges and weakens with distance.
topics.trouble: Students explain trends by saying atoms "want" full shells, instead of using charge and distance.

topics.title: Shielding and Effective Nuclear Charge
topics.short: Core electrons screen the nucleus, so a valence electron feels roughly the protons minus the core electrons.
topics.trouble: Students think electrons in the same shell shield each other as well as core electrons do.

topics.title: Successive Ionization Energies
topics.short: Each electron removed costs more, and a huge jump appears once the valence electrons are gone.
topics.trouble: Students expect the second ionization energy to be smaller than the first, or miss what the big jump says about the group.

topics.title: Exceptions in Ionization Energy
topics.short: The dips at boron and oxygen come from starting a new subshell and from the first paired electron.
topics.trouble: Students apply "ionization energy rises across a period" to every pair, missing the dips at boron and oxygen.

topics.title: Sizes of Ions
topics.short: Cations are smaller than their atoms and anions larger; in an isoelectronic series, more protons make a smaller ion.
topics.trouble: Students think the ion with more protons is the bigger one in an isoelectronic series, or that anions are smaller than their atoms.

topics.title: Potential Energy and Bond Length
topics.short: Two bonded atoms settle at the distance where their potential energy is lowest.
topics.trouble: Students think atoms are most stable when they are pushed as close together as possible.

topics.title: Lattice Energy
topics.short: Higher ion charges and smaller ions hold an ionic crystal together more tightly.
topics.trouble: Students rank lattice energies by ion size alone, missing that a 2+ and 2− pair outweighs any difference in size.

topics.title: Metals and Alloys
topics.short: Metals are cations in a sea of shared electrons; alloys mix in other atoms by substitution or in the gaps.
topics.trouble: Students think an alloy is a compound with a fixed formula, or that a metal conducts because its cations move through it.

topics.title: Formal Charge
topics.short: Assign each atom its share of the electrons; the best Lewis structure has formal charges closest to zero.
topics.trouble: Students confuse formal charge with oxidation number, or with the real charge on an atom.

topics.title: Resonance
topics.short: When more than one Lewis structure fits, the real molecule is a blend with in-between bonds.
topics.trouble: Students think the molecule flips back and forth between its resonance structures.

topics.title: Exceptions to the Octet Rule
topics.short: Odd-electron molecules, electron-poor boron and beryllium, and atoms past period 2 with more than eight electrons.
topics.trouble: Students give second-period atoms such as nitrogen more than eight electrons, or force an octet onto every atom even when the electron count is odd.

topics.title: Shapes with Five and Six Electron Groups
topics.short: The trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral families, and where their lone pairs go.
topics.trouble: Students put lone pairs in the axial positions of a trigonal bipyramid instead of the roomier equatorial ones.

topics.title: Hybrid Orbitals, Sigma and Pi Bonds
topics.short: sp, sp² and sp³ orbitals match two, three and four electron groups; a double bond is one σ bond and one π bond.
topics.trouble: Students count a double bond as two sigma bonds, or match the hybridization to the number of atoms bonded instead of the number of electron groups.

topics.title: Molecular Orbital Diagrams
topics.short: Atomic orbitals combine into bonding and antibonding orbitals that give the bond order and the magnetism.
topics.trouble: Students predict from its Lewis structure that O₂ has no unpaired electrons, missing the two in its π* orbitals that make it magnetic.

topics.title: Comparing Intermolecular Forces
topics.short: Size, polarizability and shape set the strength of dispersion forces, which can outweigh dipole forces.
topics.trouble: Students think dispersion forces are always weaker than dipole–dipole forces, so they predict that CH₃F boils higher than CCl₄.

topics.title: Vapor Pressure and Boiling
topics.short: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure above it.
topics.trouble: Students think the vapor pressure depends on how much liquid is in the container, or that water always boils at 100 °C.

topics.title: The Clausius–Clapeyron Equation
topics.short: ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁) links vapor pressure to temperature.
topics.trouble: Students use Celsius temperatures, or combine ΔH in kJ/mol with R in J/(mol·K).

topics.title: Phase Diagrams
topics.short: Read the phase at any temperature and pressure, and find the triple point and the critical point.
topics.trouble: Students read the phase from the nearest line instead of the region the point is in, or mix up the triple point and the critical point.

topics.title: Crystal Structures and Unit Cells
topics.short: Count the atoms in simple, body-centered and face-centered cubic cells, and find a crystal's density.
topics.trouble: Students count every atom drawn in a unit cell as a whole atom, forgetting that a corner atom is shared by 8 cells and a face atom by 2.

topics.title: Separating Mixtures
topics.short: Distillation sorts by boiling point, and chromatography sorts by attraction to the paper or column.
topics.trouble: Students think the spot that travels farthest in chromatography is the heaviest, instead of the one least attracted to the stationary phase.

topics.title: Electrolytes and Ions in Solution
topics.short: Strong electrolytes split completely into ions, weak electrolytes partly, and nonelectrolytes not at all.
topics.trouble: Students think soluble means strong electrolyte, or write CaCl₂ as giving Ca²⁺ and Cl₂²⁻ in water.

topics.title: Concentrations of Ions
topics.short: One formula unit can release several ions: 0.20 M CaCl₂ is 0.40 M in Cl⁻.
topics.trouble: Students give the chloride concentration as the salt's molarity, ignoring the subscript.

topics.title: The Energy of Dissolving
topics.short: Pulling solute apart and pulling solvent apart cost energy, forming new attractions releases it, and the total is ΔH of solution.
topics.trouble: Students think dissolving is always endothermic, or that a solid can dissolve only if dissolving releases heat.

topics.title: Gas Solubility and Henry's Law
topics.short: More pressure dissolves more gas (C = kP), and warmer water holds less gas.
topics.trouble: Students apply "hotter water dissolves more" to gases, which dissolve less as water warms.

topics.title: Molality, Mole Fraction and Parts per Million
topics.short: Other ways to state concentration, each suited to a different job.
topics.trouble: Students divide by liters of solution, or by the mass of the whole solution, for molality instead of by kilograms of solvent.

topics.title: Converting Concentration Units
topics.short: Use the solution's density to switch between molarity, molality and mass percent.
topics.trouble: Students treat the solution's volume in milliliters as the mass of solvent in grams, which fails for concentrated solutions.

topics.title: The Beer–Lambert Law
topics.short: Absorbance is proportional to concentration, A = εbc, so a calibration line reveals an unknown concentration.
topics.trouble: Students use percent transmittance as if it were absorbance, or think a darker solution absorbs less light.

topics.title: Vapor Pressure Lowering
topics.short: A nonvolatile solute lowers the solvent's vapor pressure: P = χ(solvent) × P°.
topics.trouble: Students use the solute's mole fraction where the solvent's belongs.

topics.title: Freezing Point Depression and Boiling Point Elevation
topics.short: ΔT = iKm: dissolved particles lower the freezing point and raise the boiling point.
topics.trouble: Students forget the van 't Hoff factor, use molarity instead of molality, or add ΔT to the freezing point.

topics.title: Osmotic Pressure
topics.short: Π = iMRT: water moves through a membrane toward the more concentrated side.
topics.trouble: Students think water flows toward the side with less solute.

topics.title: Molar Mass from Colligative Properties
topics.short: Measure ΔT or Π, find the moles of solute, then divide its mass by those moles.
topics.trouble: Students divide by the mass of solvent instead of the moles of solute, or forget to change grams of solvent to kilograms.

topics.title: Gas Density and Molar Mass
topics.short: d = PM/RT, so the density of a gas reveals its molar mass.
topics.trouble: Students think a gas has a fixed density like a solid, ignoring temperature and pressure.

topics.title: Gas Stoichiometry
topics.short: Use PV = nRT to turn a volume of gas into moles inside a stoichiometry problem.
topics.trouble: Students use 22.4 L/mol at conditions that are not 0 °C and 1 atm.

topics.title: Partial Pressures and Mole Fractions
topics.short: Each gas in a mixture pushes as if it were alone: Pᵢ = χᵢ × P(total).
topics.trouble: Students think the gas with heavier molecules supplies more of the pressure, or forget to subtract water's vapor pressure for a gas collected over water.

topics.title: Molecular Speeds and Effusion
topics.short: At one temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy, so lighter molecules move faster and effuse faster: rate ∝ 1/√M.
topics.trouble: Students think heavier molecules have more kinetic energy at the same temperature, or forget the square root in Graham's law.

topics.title: The Maxwell–Boltzmann Distribution
topics.short: Molecular speeds spread over a curve that flattens and shifts toward faster speeds as the temperature rises.
topics.trouble: Students think the peak of the curve gets taller at a higher temperature, when it gets lower and wider.

topics.title: Real Gases
topics.short: The particles' own volume and their attractions make real gases stray from PV = nRT at high pressure and low temperature.
topics.trouble: Students think real gases stray most at high temperature and low pressure, the very conditions where they behave most ideally.

topics.title: Net Ionic Equations
topics.short: Write dissolved strong electrolytes as ions, then cancel the spectator ions.
topics.trouble: Students split solids, water, gases or weak acids into ions, or leave spectator ions in the net equation.

topics.title: Solution Stoichiometry
topics.short: Molarity times volume gives moles, which go straight into a mole ratio.
topics.trouble: Students multiply molarity by milliliters as if they were liters, or skip the mole ratio.

topics.title: Gravimetric Analysis
topics.short: Weigh a precipitate to find how much of an ion a sample held.
topics.trouble: Students take the precipitate's mass as the mass of the ion, forgetting to multiply by the ion's share of the precipitate's mass.

topics.title: Titration Calculations
topics.short: Use the volume at the equivalence point and the mole ratio to find a concentration, a molar mass or a percent purity.
topics.trouble: Students divide the moles of acid by the volume of base used instead of the volume of the acid sample.

topics.title: Oxidation Numbers
topics.short: Oxidation numbers are bookkeeping charges that track electrons; in a neutral compound they add to zero.
topics.trouble: Students give every atom in a polyatomic ion the ion's charge, or forget that the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound add to zero.

topics.title: Oxidation and Reduction
topics.short: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain; one never happens without the other.
topics.trouble: Students call the substance that gets oxidized the oxidizing agent.

topics.title: Balancing Redox Reactions
topics.short: Split the reaction into half-reactions, balance atoms and charge with electrons, then add them back together.
topics.trouble: Students balance the atoms but not the charge, or add H⁺ in a basic solution and never change it to OH⁻.

topics.title: Redox Titrations
topics.short: Titrate with permanganate or another oxidizing agent, using the electron-balanced mole ratio.
topics.trouble: Students use a 1 : 1 ratio as in simple acid–base titrations, instead of the 5 : 1 ratio of Fe²⁺ to MnO₄⁻.

topics.title: The First Law and Sign Conventions
topics.short: ΔU = q + w: energy that enters the system counts as positive, and energy that leaves counts as negative.
topics.trouble: Students mix the physics and chemistry sign conventions for work, or give q a positive sign when the system loses heat.

topics.title: Pressure–Volume Work
topics.short: A gas that expands against an outside pressure does work on the surroundings: w = −PΔV.
topics.trouble: Students drop the minus sign, so an expanding gas seems to gain energy, or forget that 1 L·atm = 101.3 J.

topics.title: Enthalpy and Thermochemical Equations
topics.short: ΔH is the heat at constant pressure; it scales with the equation and changes sign when the reaction is reversed.
topics.trouble: Students keep the sign of ΔH when they reverse a reaction, or forget to double ΔH when they double the coefficients.

topics.title: Heat from Amounts of Reactant
topics.short: Multiply moles by ΔH per mole of reaction, using the mole ratio to the substance you were given.
topics.trouble: Students multiply ΔH by grams instead of moles, or by the moles of a substance that has a different coefficient.

topics.title: Heat for Warming and Phase Changes Together
topics.short: Add mcΔT for each warming step and nΔH for each phase change along the way.
topics.trouble: Students use liquid water's specific heat for ice and steam too, or leave out the phase-change steps.

topics.title: Calorimetry for Reactions
topics.short: Find ΔH from a temperature change: q(reaction) = −q(solution), divided by the moles that reacted.
topics.trouble: Students report q of the solution as ΔH without changing its sign or dividing by the moles of the limiting reactant.

topics.title: Bomb Calorimetry
topics.short: At constant volume, the heat the calorimeter takes up, C(cal) × ΔT, measures the energy released by burning a sample.
topics.trouble: Students use water's specific heat and a mass when the calorimeter's heat capacity is given in kJ/°C.

topics.title: Hess's Law
topics.short: Add chemical equations like algebra, and add their ΔH values the same way.
topics.trouble: Students reverse or scale an equation but forget to do the same to its ΔH.

topics.title: Standard Enthalpies of Formation
topics.short: ΔH°(reaction) = Σ ΔH°f(products) − Σ ΔH°f(reactants).
topics.trouble: Students subtract in the wrong order, or forget that an element in its standard state, such as O₂(g), has ΔH°f = 0.

topics.title: Born–Haber Cycles
topics.short: Add up the steps that build an ionic solid from its elements to find its lattice energy.
topics.trouble: Students forget to take half the bond energy of Cl₂, or leave out magnesium's second ionization energy when forming Mg²⁺.
